common_name: Kew Passionflower (Historic Kew Gardens Hybrid Vine)

planting.note: Set out cutting-grown vines after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun; this hybrid inherits fragrance from its winged-stem parent along with the vigor of blue passionflower.

directions: Raised at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew from a cross between the fragrant winged-stem passionflower and cold-hardy blue passionflower, this hybrid combines a sweeter scent than plain blue passionflower with somewhat larger flowers banded in blue, white, and purple across the corona filaments. It grows vigorously once established and flowers over a long summer season, drawing bees steadily to a sunny trellis or fence. Because one parent is a true tropical, it carries less cold hardiness than straight blue passionflower and typically dies back hard after freezing weather, so mulch the crown well before winter in the cooler part of its range. Prune out dead top growth in spring once new shoots appear from the base.

common_name: Caeruleoracemosa Passionflower (Red-Flowered Blue Hybrid Vine, Parent of Lady Margaret)

planting.note: Set out cutting-grown vines after the last frost in well-drained soil in full sun; this hybrid between blue passionflower and red passionflower is the parent of several later red-flowered hybrids including Lady Margaret.

directions: A cross between blue passionflower and the tropical red passionflower, this hybrid produces clusters of small red to red-purple flowers held in loose racemes rather than the single blooms typical of most passionflower hybrids, a trait it passes on to its own well-known offspring, Lady Margaret. It is grown today mainly by breeders and collectors maintaining historic passionflower lineages, though it makes an attractive vine in its own right on a sunny trellis or fence. Like other hybrids carrying a tropical parent, it dies back hard after freezing weather and regrows from the base once temperatures warm, so mulch the crown heavily going into winter. Give it full sun and average, well-drained soil, and expect steady summer bloom that attracts pollinators.

planting.note: Set out cutting-grown vines only once nights stay reliably above 55°F; this hybrid of blue passionflower and a tender giant granadilla parent has little cold tolerance and needs a long warm season to flower well.

directions: Raised in France from a cross between blue passionflower and a large-flowered tropical granadilla, this vigorous hybrid produces big, fragrant flowers in shades of pink and lavender with a boldly banded purple-and-white corona, larger and showier than plain blue passionflower. Its tropical parentage makes it noticeably more heat-loving and considerably less cold-hardy, so it performs best where summers are long and warm and struggles anywhere winter temperatures drop much below freezing. Provide a sturdy arbor or pergola to support its rampant climbing habit, and grow it in a large container that can be moved under cover for winter outside the warmest zones. Hand pollination between flowers may improve fruit set, though it is grown chiefly for its striking, fragrant blooms.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil; site in full sun for the strongest gold color, since shade fades the foliage toward green.

directions: One of the oldest golden-leaved selections of European black elder, Aurea holds a bright yellow-gold leaf color through the growing season wherever it gets ample sun, fading toward chartreuse-green in shadier spots. Flat clusters of creamy white, musky-scented flowers open in early summer against the gold foliage, followed by the same glossy black berries produced by the wild species. It stands apart from the golden-leaved American elder sold under the same cultivar name, being a distinct, longer-established European selection with a fuller, broader-leaved look. Renewal-prune the oldest stems each winter to keep a steady supply of vigorous young growth, since the best gold color develops on this season's canes.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs
